analysis.one_liner: Balances the budget in seven years by cutting Medicare, Medicaid, welfare, and food stamps while trimming capital gains taxes.
analysis.headline: Both chambers passed it by narrow party-line votes — the House twice and the Senate twice — but President Clinton vetoed it on December 6, 1995, and it never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: This was the huge reconciliation bill House Republicans wrote in 1995 to carry out their plan to balance the budget in seven years. It would have replaced Medicaid with block grants to states, restructured Medicare around private plans, replaced federal welfare with state block grants, tightened food stamps, and raised the debt limit. To help pay for it, it also cut taxes on capital gains, estates, and retirement savings, opened the Arctic Refuge and other federal land to mining, oil, and grazing interests, and curtailed the government's direct student loan program.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households, through a 50% capital gains deduction, indexing of assets held over three years, larger estate and gift exemptions, restored IRA deductions, and tax-free medical savings accounts [S3]. Working families would get a $500 per-child credit, a bigger standard deduction for married couples, an adoption credit, and a deduction for student loan interest [S3]. Health insurers and HMOs would gain a large new market under the MedicarePlus program and state Medicaid contracting; banks and thrifts would get relief from Community Reinvestment Act obligations; mining, oil and gas, grazing, and ski interests would gain cheaper access to federal land and assets; student loan guarantee companies would keep their role as the government retreated from direct lending [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Higher-income households, insurers, banks, mining and oil interests

how_it_helps.text: Creates a $500 per-child tax credit, raises the standard deduction for married couples, allows a credit of up to $5,000 for adoption expenses, and allows a deduction of up to $2,500 for student loan interest [S3].

Cuts the tax rate on capital gains roughly in half for individuals through a 50% deduction and indexes the basis of assets held more than three years to inflation, and restores and expands IRA deductions [S3].

Restructures Medicare into a 'MedicarePlus' program giving beneficiaries a choice of private health plans and a high-deductible plan with a medical savings account, and adds a surcharge on Part B premiums for beneficiaries with high incomes [S3].
Replaces the open-ended federal Medicaid entitlement with fixed block grants to states, and replaces the AFDC welfare program with block grants carrying mandatory work requirements [S3].
Raises the public debt limit to $5.5 trillion as part of the balanced-budget plan [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Low-income families and children, who would lose the federal Medicaid entitlement, the AFDC cash guarantee, and parts of the food stamp and earned income tax credit programs [S2] [S3]. Seniors would face limits on Medicare payment growth, a 13% Part B premium increase, and a $4 veterans' drug copayment [S3]. Construction workers on federal projects would lose prevailing-wage protection under the House-passed Davis-Bacon repeal [S2]. Students would lose access to the direct federal loan program, which would be capped at a small share of loans [S3]. Low-income neighborhoods would lose leverage over banks' community lending under the weakened Community Reinvestment Act [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-income families, seniors, students, federal construction workers

drawbacks.text: The MediGrant block grant would terminate Medicaid's federal guarantee: the bill states that no individual would have an entitlement to medical assistance under federal law and no person could sue a state over compliance, leaving coverage to state plans and fixed funding [S3].

The welfare title replaces AFDC with block grants that deny aid to families without a minor child, teenage parents not in school or in adult-supervised settings, and adults who refuse work, with pro rata benefit cuts for refusal to work [S3].

Food stamp changes would cut off non-exempt adults who received benefits four or more months in a year without working 20 hours a week, cap the excludable value of a car at $4,600, and make many legal immigrants ineligible for SSI, food stamps, and Medicaid for five years after entry [S3].
The earned income credit would be repealed outright for workers without children and its phaseout raised, cutting a wage subsidy for the working poor [S2] [S3].

The tax side cuts taxes concentrated among higher-income households — capital gains, estates, and investment income — even while reducing spending on health and income security for the poor, making the package harder to defend on fairness grounds [S3].

The House-passed bill repealed the Davis-Bacon Act and the Service Contract Act, eliminating the requirement that workers on federally funded construction and service contracts be paid locally prevailing wages [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The family tax credits and the debt-limit/balanced-budget framing were real, and some Medicare changes (like the oral breast-cancer drug coverage and income-related Part B premiums) cut in a progressive direction [S3]. But the package's largest and most certain effects ran the other way: fixed block grants replacing Medicaid's guarantee, welfare and food stamp cuts, repeal of the childless-worker earned income credit, and prevailing-wage repeal would have shifted risk onto the people least able to bear it, while the capital gains and estate provisions concentrated their benefits at the top [S2] [S3]. On balance the bill asked more of low-income families, seniors, and students than of the households and industries that gained most from its tax and resource provisions.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it, the Senate passed its own version, a conference committee patched the two together, and both chambers approved the final product — but President Clinton vetoed it on December 6, 1995, and no override vote followed, so it died.

narrative.text: The House Committee on the Budget reported the original measure on October 17, 1995, and the House passed it on October 26 by 227-203 — 223 of 233 Republicans in favor, 192 of 199 Democrats opposed [S6] [S8].
The Senate substituted its own budget reconciliation text and passed it 52-47 on October 28, with all 52 Republicans in favor and all 46 Democrats opposed [S6] [S9].

House Democrats failed 180-250 on a motion to recommit that would have protected the health and income security of seniors and children, denied tax reductions for upper-income families, and retained federal retirement provisions for Members of Congress [S6] [S7].

A Democratic motion to instruct House conferees to minimize tax cuts for the wealthy and protect seniors' health security failed 198-219, with 191 of 199 Democrats in favor and only 6 of 232 Republicans [S6] [S10].

The conference report was approved by the House 237-189 on November 17; a Senate point of order against it was sustained after a Budget Act waiver failed 54-45, so the Senate instead receded from its amendment and concurred 52-47 [S15] [S16] [S17].
The House agreed to the Senate amendment 235-192 on November 20, again with 230 of 233 Republicans in favor and 190 of 198 Democrats opposed [S6] [S18].

The bill was presented to the President on November 30, 1995, and vetoed on December 6, 1995; the House then simply referred the bill and veto message to the Budget Committee, and the 104th Congress ended without it becoming law [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seniors, low-income families, and students kept the existing Medicaid guarantee, welfare and food stamp rules, prevailing-wage protections, and direct loan program that the bill would have cut. The industries that stood to gain from its tax cuts, deregulation, and federal resource sell-offs did not get them, and the deficit was not reduced by this measure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seniors and low-income families who kept existing protections

sides.party_line_note: Every major vote split by party: House passage 223-4 among Republicans versus 4-192 among Democrats, Senate passage 52-1 among Republicans versus 0-46 among Democrats, and the final House concurrence 230-1 versus 5-190 — followed by a Democratic president's veto.

industries.note: MedicarePlus would open Medicare to competing private plans with capped capitation payments, and the Medicaid block grants would let states contract with HMOs and other managed-care organizations as program providers. This creates a permanent, publicly funded customer base for private insurers even as it constrains program spending [S3].

The 50% capital gains deduction, indexing for assets held over three years, larger estate and gift exemptions, restored IRA deductions, and medical savings accounts concentrate their benefits among households with capital gains and large estates, while the bill's spending cuts fall on low-income programs [S3].

The bill exempts institutions with $100 million or less in assets from Community Reinvestment Act evaluation, allows self-certification for some institutions up to $250 million, and bars regulators from imposing additional recordkeeping — reducing the obligations banks face to lend in low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. It also merges deposit insurance funds and phases out the federal thrift charter [S2].

industries.industry: Student loan guarantee companies and FFEL lenders
industries.note: The bill caps the federal Direct Loan program at 10% of new loan volume and limits participation to the 102 institutions already enrolled, effectively entrenching the lender-and-guarantee-agency system as the main channel for federal student loans [S3].

The bill replaces near-free patenting with a royalty of 3.5% (House) or 5% (Senate) of net proceeds on minerals taken from federal land, plus modest annual claim rentals — a fraction of what comparable royalties run, and it dedicates part of the proceeds to abandoned-mine cleanup [S2] [S3].

The bill opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to leasing while declaring environmental reviews already satisfied, suspends royalties for seven years on new deepwater Gulf leases, and allows Alaskan North Slope oil exports, subject to a presidential national-interest finding [S3].

The House-passed bill repealed the Davis-Bacon Act and the Service Contract Act, letting contractors on federally funded construction and service work pay below locally prevailing wages — a direct cost to the workers on those jobs [S2].

The bill extends deficiency payments, marketing loans, and planting flexibility for wheat, feed grains, cotton, rice, and oilseeds through 2002 while cutting payment rates and phasing down dairy and sugar supports, and it preserves the peanut quota program at $628 per ton [S3].
